unit.title: Prepare and install basic cable trays

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before you install a cable tray, which document tells you the route, the tray size and the fixing height?
options: The cable maker's price list
The job drawing and specification
The sign-in register at the site gate
The tool store sign-out book

questions.stem: Why should you walk the tray route on site before you order the materials?
options: To find the shortest way to the tool store
To count how many workers are on site that day
To choose the paint colour for the walls nearby
To check for beams, pipes and ducts in the way

questions.stem: Which PPE (personal protective equipment) protects your hands from the sharp cut edges of a steel tray?
options: Cut-resistant work gloves
Thin disposable plastic gloves
Woollen knitted gloves
Rubber kitchen gloves

questions.stem: You are cutting a steel tray with a hacksaw. What should you wear to protect your eyes?
options: Sunglasses with dark lenses
A welding helmet
Safety glasses
Reading glasses

questions.stem: A tray is to be fixed 3 m above the floor. What is the safest way to reach it for most of the work?
options: Stand on a stack of empty cable drums and boxes
Use a mobile tower scaffold with guard rails
Stand on the top step of a stepladder
Climb up and sit on the bracket arms

questions.stem: What must you check before you use a ladder?
options: That the stiles, rungs and feet are sound
That it is the lightest ladder in the store today
That it is painted the same colour as the tray
That it has been used on this site before

questions.stem: A tray run passes over a walkway. What should you do while you work overhead?
options: Work quickly so that nobody walks under you
Ask a friend to shout if someone comes near
Leave your tools on the tray so they are in reach
Barrier off the area below and put up signs

questions.stem: Which type of cable tray has two side rails joined by rungs?
options: Solid-bottom tray
Perforated tray
Ladder tray
Cable trunking

questions.stem: Which tray gives good support along the length of small cables and still lets air flow through?
options: Perforated tray
Ladder tray with wide rung spacing
Solid-bottom tray with a cover
A single hook hanger

questions.stem: When is a solid-bottom tray with a cover a good choice?
options: When the cables must carry the very highest current
When cables need protection from dust and falling objects
When the tray must be as light as possible to lift
When the run is very short and straight

questions.stem: A tray will be fixed outdoors near the sea in Port Antonio. Which material resists corrosion best?
options: Plain mild steel with no coating
Untreated pine timber battens
Stainless steel or fibreglass
Mild steel with one coat of household paint

questions.stem: What does "hot-dip galvanised" mean for a steel tray?
options: It was heated to make it softer to bend
It was painted with a heat-proof paint
It was dipped in plastic to insulate it
It was coated in zinc to stop rust

questions.stem: Where do you find the largest distance allowed between the supports of a tray?
options: On the label of the cable drum
In the tray maker's load and span tables
In the building's fire escape plan
On the weekly time sheet kept for the job

questions.stem: What can happen if tray supports are spaced too far apart?
options: The tray can sag or bend under the cables
The cables will carry less current through the run
The tray will rust much more quickly
The cables will be easier to pull in

questions.stem: Which fixing is used to hang a tray support from a steel beam without drilling the beam?
options: Plastic wall plugs with screws
Steel nails and a club hammer
A beam clamp
Construction adhesive only

questions.stem: What is slotted metal strut channel used for in a tray installation?
options: To join two lengths of tray end to end
To cover the cables on top of the tray
To earth the tray back to the main panel
To make brackets and hanger supports

questions.stem: Which tool do you use to drill holes in a concrete ceiling?
options: A rotary hammer drill with a masonry bit
A hand drill with a flat wood bit
A cordless screwdriver with a metal-cutting bit
A pillar drill with a hole saw

questions.stem: Which tool helps you mark a level line for a long tray run on a wall?
options: A tri-square and a pencil
A laser level or chalk line
A plumb bob
A long steel rule and a pencil

questions.stem: A straight run must be 4.5 m long. The tray comes in 3 m lengths. What is the fewest number of lengths you need?
Why should a length of tray be clamped or held firm before you cut it?
options: So the saw blade stays cool during the cut
So that the zinc coating does not come off
So it cannot move, and the cut is straight and safe
So that you can cut it with one hand

questions.stem: Why must you remove the burrs from the cut edges of a tray?
options: So burrs do not cut cable sheaths or your hands
So the tray is a little lighter to lift and carry
So the cut end shines like the factory edge
So the splice bolts need less tightening

questions.stem: How are two straight lengths of ladder tray joined end to end?
options: With cable ties wrapped round the side rails
With splice plates and the maker's bolts
By tack welding the rungs together on site
With binding wire twisted round both rails

questions.stem: When you bolt a splice plate, which way round do the bolts usually go?
options: Nuts inside the tray, facing the cables
Either way round, it does not matter
Bolt heads inside the tray, nuts outside
No bolts; the plates just push on

questions.stem: Which fitting is used where a tray must turn 90° and stay on the same level?
options: A riser
A reducer
A four-way cross fitting
A horizontal bend

questions.stem: Which fitting is used where a tray must go up or down to a new level?
options: A vertical bend (riser)
A horizontal tee fitting
A straight reducer
A straight coupler

questions.stem: What does a reducer fitting do?
options: Fixes the end of a tray to a wall
Lowers the weight of the tray run
Joins a wide tray to a narrower one
Cuts down the number of supports

questions.stem: Why must a metal cable tray be connected to earth (ground)?
options: So the tray can carry the neutral current back
So that a fault to the tray will trip the protection
So that the cables in the tray run much cooler
So rain runs off it and the tray does not rust

questions.stem: At a tray joint where the splice plate may not give a good electrical path, what is fitted?
options: A plastic spacer between the ends
An extra cable tie around the joint
A wrap of insulating tape
A bonding jumper across the joint

questions.stem: How do you check that the earth path is good from one end of a tray run to the other?
options: A continuity test with a low-resistance ohmmeter
Tapping the tray with a spanner to hear if it rings
Looking to see that it is all the same colour
Measuring the length of the run with a tape

questions.stem: How should cables be laid in a tray?
options: Twisted together in a bundle to save space
Piled loosely in any order to save time
Neatly side by side, with few crossings
Pulled tight so they lift off the rungs

questions.stem: What can happen if a tray holds more cables than the maker allows?
options: The cables will pull in faster and easier
The cables can overheat and the tray may sag
The circuit breakers will trip less often
The cable insulation will last much longer

questions.stem: Why are power cables and data cables kept apart in a tray?
options: Data cables are heavier and need more room
Power cables need more light to be seen
Data cables run hotter than power cables
Power cables can cause interference on data

questions.stem: Why must cables on a vertical tray run be fixed at regular spacing?
options: So their own weight does not strain them
So that the cables can carry more current
So that the tray needs fewer supports
So the cables can be slid out later on

questions.stem: Why must you keep to a cable's minimum bending radius at a tray bend?
options: So the run uses less cable from the drum overall
To avoid damage to the conductors and insulation
So that the bend looks neat to the customer
So that the cable labels can be read easily

questions.stem: Where cables leave the tray to drop down to equipment, what protects them at the tray edge?
options: A cable tie pulled tight against the edge
Nothing; the cable sheath is strong enough
A drop-out fitting or smooth edge guard
A wrap of masking tape on the side rail

questions.stem: A cable schedule is a list for the job. What does it show?
options: The pay rate of each worker on the job
The address and phone number of the tray maker
The opening and closing hours of the site
Each cable's size, type, route and end points

questions.stem: The tray passes through a fire-rated wall. What must be done to the opening once the cables are in?
options: Seal it with an approved fire-stopping material
Leave it open so that the cables can stay cool
Pack it with cardboard and cover it with tape
Fill it with any foam from the hardware store

questions.stem: How should two people carry a 3 m length of tray?
options: One person drags it by one end along the floor
Both hold the middle and walk along sideways
One at each end, knees bent, back straight
One carries it upright through the doorways

questions.stem: After fixing, how do you check that a tray run is straight and level?
options: By eye, looking up from the floor only
With a spirit level or laser along the run
By asking the customer what they think
By pushing the tray to see if it moves

questions.stem: On your final check of a tray run, which of these is a fault you must put right?
options: Splice bolts tight and all in place
Supports at the spacing on the drawing
Cables neatly laid and tied in
A bracket with a missing anchor bolt

questions.stem: What should you do with tray off-cuts and metal filings at the end of the job?
options: Collect them and put them in the scrap metal bin
Leave them in the tray for the next trade to move
Sweep them under the nearest cupboard
Leave them on the floor for the cleaners

questions.stem: The tray route on the drawing clashes with a new water pipe. What should you do?
options: Move the water pipe yourself to clear the way
Fix the tray so that it rests on the pipe
Stop and report it so a new route can be agreed
Change the route yourself and say nothing

questions.stem: Which tool tightens splice plate nuts to the torque the maker states?
options: A pipe wrench
A torque wrench
An adjustable spanner
Slip-joint pliers from the kit

questions.stem: Why is a support usually placed close to each tray fitting, such as a bend or a tee?
options: So the fitting is easier to paint
So the cable labels can be fixed onto the support arm
So that fewer splice bolts are needed
Fittings are weak points if left unsupported

questions.stem: A tray bracket must be fixed close to an existing cable in the wall. What must be done first?
options: Drill slowly and carefully so you miss it
Wet the wall so that the drill bit runs cooler
Isolate, lock off, tag and prove the circuit dead
Wrap the drill handle in insulating tape

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: A tray is to be fixed 3 m above a busy workshop floor. Describe how you would work safely at that height.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would choose the right access equipment, such as a mobile scaffold tower with guard rails and toe boards, or a podium step for lower parts. I would check that it is complete and not damaged, build it on firm, level ground as the maker's instructions say, and lock the wheels before anyone climbs. I would never stand on the top step of a ladder or on boxes or drums. Below the work, I would put up barriers and warning signs so that nobody walks under me. Tools and fixings would be kept in a bag or tray on the platform so they cannot fall. I would wear a hard hat, safety boots and gloves. I would not over-reach; I would climb down and move the tower instead. Long tray lengths would be lifted up by two people, and a supervisor would be told before the work starts.
markingPoints: Chooses suitable access, such as a mobile tower with guard rails, not boxes or the top of a ladder
Checks the equipment and sets it up on level ground with wheels locked
Barriers and signs below so nobody walks under the work
Stops tools and materials falling (tool bag, tray on platform) and wears hard hat and boots
Does not over-reach; moves the tower; two people lift long lengths

essays.stem: Explain the steps you would take to plan a cable tray installation before you start work on site.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by reading the drawings, the specification and the cable schedule to find the route, the tray type and width, the height and the number of cables. Then I would walk the route on site with a tape and check for beams, pipes, ducts and fire walls that are in the way, and note where bends, tees and risers are needed. I would check the maker's tables for the support spacing and the load the tray can carry. From this I would make a list of tray lengths, fittings, splice plates, bolts, supports, anchors and bonding jumpers, adding a little extra for waste. I would list the tools and the access equipment needed, such as a tower scaffold. I would think about the hazards, such as work at height, sharp edges, drilling near existing cables and dust, and write down how to control them. Finally, I would agree the plan and any clashes with my supervisor.
markingPoints: Reads drawings, specification and cable schedule for route, size and height
Walks the route and notes obstacles and the fittings needed
Uses the maker's tables for support spacing and load
Makes a materials and tools list, including access equipment
Identifies hazards and controls, and agrees the plan with the supervisor

essays.stem: Compare ladder tray, perforated tray and wire mesh (basket) tray. Say where each type is best used.
essays.modelAnswer: Ladder tray has two strong side rails joined by rungs. It is strong, carries heavy loads over long spans and lets plenty of air reach the cables, so it is used for large power cables, for example in a factory or a hotel plant room. Small cables can sag between the rungs, so it is less suited to them. Perforated tray has a flat base with holes punched in it. The base supports small cables along their whole length, and the holes let air through and give places to fix ties. It is used for mixed small power and control cables. Wire mesh or basket tray is made from welded steel wire. It is light, easy to cut and bend on site, and lets air through. It is often used for data and small cables above ceilings in offices and shops. For all types the maker's load tables decide the support spacing.
markingPoints: Ladder tray: rails and rungs, strong, long spans, good for large cables
Perforated tray: flat base with holes, supports small cables along their length
Wire mesh tray: light, easy to cut and shape, often for data cables above ceilings
Mentions air flow (ventilation) and the load each can carry
Gives a sensible place of use for each type

essays.stem: Describe how you would mark out and fix the wall brackets for a straight tray run along a concrete wall.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check the drawing for the height and the route, and make sure there are no hidden cables or pipes where I will drill, using a cable detector and isolating any circuit that is close. I would mark a level line along the wall at the right height with a laser level or a chalk line. Next I would mark the bracket positions along the line, using the spacing from the tray maker's tables and putting a bracket close to each end and near any fitting. I would drill each hole with a hammer drill and a masonry bit of the size the anchor maker states, wearing safety glasses, a dust mask and ear protection. I would blow out the dust, fit the anchors and bolt the brackets on, keeping them square and level. Finally I would check the brackets with a level and string line before laying the tray on.
markingPoints: Checks the drawing and checks for hidden cables or pipes before drilling
Marks a level line with a laser or chalk line at the right height
Sets bracket spacing from the maker's tables, with brackets near ends and fittings
Drills with the correct bit and anchor, wearing eye, dust and ear protection
Fixes brackets square and level, then checks the line

essays.stem: Describe how you would cut a length of galvanised steel tray to size and join it into the run.
essays.modelAnswer: I would measure the gap on site, mark the length on the tray with a square so that the cut is straight, and check the measurement again. I would clamp the tray firmly and cut it with a hacksaw or a suitable power saw, wearing safety glasses and gloves. On ladder tray I would cut where the maker allows so the length keeps its strength. Next I would file off all the burrs so the edges cannot cut cables or hands. The cut edge has lost its zinc, so I would coat it with zinc-rich (cold galvanising) paint to stop rust. Then I would line up the cut length with the run, fit the splice plates on each side, and put the bolts in with the heads inside the tray and the nuts outside. I would tighten the nuts to the torque the maker states and fit a bonding jumper if the joint needs one.
markingPoints: Measures, marks square and checks again before cutting
Clamps the tray and cuts with a suitable saw, wearing eye protection and gloves
Removes burrs from the cut edge
Treats the cut edge with zinc-rich paint to stop rust
Joins with splice plates, bolt heads inside, tightened to the maker's torque, with bonding if needed

essays.stem: Explain why a metal cable tray must be earthed, and how you make sure the earth path is continuous along the whole run.
essays.modelAnswer: If a cable is damaged, its live conductor can touch the metal tray. If the tray is not earthed, the tray could become live and give a shock to anyone who touches it. When the tray is connected to earth, the fault current flows back through the earth path and the fuse or circuit breaker operates quickly, cutting off the supply. To make the earth path continuous, every joint must give a good connection. I would clean the contact faces, fit the splice plates with all the bolts and tighten them to the maker's torque. Where a joint may not give a good path, such as at a painted surface, an expansion joint or a hinged fitting, I would fit a bonding jumper across it. I would connect the tray to the main earth with a protective conductor of the right size. With the circuits isolated, I would test continuity from end to end with a low-resistance ohmmeter.
markingPoints: A fault can make an unearthed tray live and cause a shock
The earth path lets fault current flow so the protection operates
Clean, tight splice joints with all bolts fitted
Bonding jumpers across joints that may not conduct, and a connection to the main earth
Continuity test end to end with a low-resistance ohmmeter

essays.stem: Describe good practice when laying and fixing cables in a tray.
essays.modelAnswer: Before laying cables I would check that the tray is complete, earthed and free of burrs and sharp edges. I would use the cable schedule to lay each cable in its planned place, and label both ends. Cables are laid neatly side by side, with as few crossings as possible, and they are not twisted or pulled tight. Power cables are kept apart from data and control cables, using a divider or a separate tray, to reduce interference. I would keep to each cable's minimum bending radius at bends and risers so that the conductors and insulation are not damaged. On horizontal runs the cables are tied in at regular spacing, and on vertical runs they are tied or cleated more often so that their weight does not strain them. I would not fill the tray beyond what the maker allows, so that the cables do not overheat. Where cables leave the tray, a drop-out fitting or edge guard protects them.
markingPoints: Checks the tray first and lays cables to the schedule, with labels
Neat and side by side, few crossings, not twisted or pulled tight
Keeps power and data apart
Keeps to the bending radius and protects cables where they leave the tray
Ties at regular spacing (closer on vertical runs) and does not overfill

essays.stem: An old light fitting on the tray route must be taken down before you can fix the tray. Describe how you would isolate its circuit safely.
essays.modelAnswer: I would never work on a circuit while it is live. First I would find the right circuit from the panel schedule and tell the people who use the area that the power will be off. I would switch off the circuit breaker or remove the fuse, then fit a lock to the breaker so it cannot be switched on, and fix a tag with my name, the date and the reason. I keep the key with me. Next I would check my voltage tester on a known live source or a proving unit to show it is working. Then I would test at the light fitting between all the conductors, live to neutral, live to earth and neutral to earth, to prove it is dead. After that I would check the tester again on the known source to show it did not fail during the test. Only then would I start work, following the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Identifies the correct circuit and tells the people affected
Switches off and locks off the breaker or removes the fuse
Fixes a tag and keeps the key
Checks the tester on a known live source or proving unit before the test
Proves dead between all conductors, then checks the tester again after the test

essays.stem: Describe how you would inspect a finished tray installation before you hand it over.
essays.modelAnswer: I would walk the full run with the drawing and check that the route, height and tray size are what was asked for. I would check that the run is straight and level with a spirit level or laser, and that every support is at the right spacing, with all anchors and bolts in place and tight. At each joint I would check that the splice plates have all their bolts, that bolt heads face the cables, and that bonding jumpers are fitted where needed. I would look for burrs and sharp edges, and check that cut edges are painted. I would check that cables are laid neatly, tied in, labelled, not overfilled and protected where they leave the tray, and that fire-stopping is done where the tray passes through fire walls. With the circuits isolated, I would test the earth continuity of the tray. Any fault would be put right, and the results written on the job report.
markingPoints: Checks route, height and size against the drawing
Checks straight and level, support spacing, anchors and bolts tight
Checks joints, bonding jumpers, burrs and painted cut edges
Checks cables neat, tied, labelled, not overfilled; fire-stopping done
Tests earth continuity and records results and repairs

essays.stem: Describe what you would do at the end of a cable tray job to finish, clean up and report.
essays.modelAnswer: When the tray is complete and checked, I would make sure every bolt is tight and every end cap and cover is fitted. I would collect all off-cuts, bolts and metal filings and put metal in the scrap bin and other rubbish in the right bins, so that nothing is left on the tray or the floor. Dust from drilling would be swept or vacuumed. I would take down barriers and the tower scaffold only when the work above is finished, and return the tools and access equipment to the store, reporting any damage. Unused materials would be counted and returned. Then I would mark any changes to the route on the drawing so the customer has a true record, and fill in the job report with the work done, the materials used, the test results and any problem left for others. Finally I would tell my supervisor the job is ready to hand over.
markingPoints: Final check that fixings are tight and end caps or covers are fitted
Collects off-cuts and filings into the right bins; sweeps up dust
Returns tools and access equipment, reports any damage, returns spare materials
Marks changes on the drawing (as-fitted record)
Completes the job report and tells the supervisor

practical1.title: Install a wall-mounted ladder tray run with a horizontal bend
practical1.brief: As a group, install a run of ladder tray on the training bay wall, about 2 m long, with one 90° horizontal bend and a splice joint, as shown on the instructor's drawing. Mark a level line, fix cantilever brackets at the spacing given, cut one length to size, deburr and paint the cut edge, join the lengths with splice plates and fit a bonding jumper. No circuits on the bay are live; if the instructor says a circuit near the work must be isolated, the group shows safe isolation before drilling. Share the work so that every member marks out, drills and fixes at least one bracket, and helps with the cut, the joint and the continuity test. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the run is finished and the area is clean.
materials: Ladder tray, 2 lengths, with one 90° horizontal bend (width as on the drawing)
Splice plates, nuts and bolts, and one bonding jumper
Cantilever wall brackets with anchors to suit the wall
Hammer drill and masonry bits; hacksaw, file and zinc-rich paint
Laser level or chalk line, spirit level, tape measure, square
Step platform or mobile tower as the Centre provides
photos: The level line and bracket positions marked on the wall
Brackets fixed, with a spirit level on them
The cut length, deburred, with the cut edge painted
The splice joint, bolt heads inside the tray, and the bonding jumper
The finished run with the bend, from the front
The continuity test being done from end to end, showing the reading
The work area cleaned, with off-cuts in the scrap bin
checklist: Wore safety glasses, gloves and boots; used ear and dust protection when drilling
Marked a level line and bracket positions to the drawing and spacing given
Drilled and fixed brackets square, level and secure
Cut the tray square, removed burrs and painted the cut edge
Fitted splice plates with all bolts, heads inside, tightened to the maker's torque
Fitted the bonding jumper and took part in the continuity test
Used the access equipment safely and kept the area below clear
Left the area clean, returned tools and reported any damage
safety: Check for hidden cables before drilling; any nearby circuit is isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead first
Wear safety glasses when cutting and drilling, and gloves when handling cut tray
Use the step platform or tower as the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules say; never stand on boxes
Two people lift and carry each tray length
Keep the floor below clear and put up a barrier while work is overhead

practical2.title: Install a perforated tray on trapeze hangers with a tee, and lay cables
practical2.brief: As a group, hang a perforated tray from the training bay ceiling frame on trapeze hangers made from threaded rod and strut channel. The run is about 2 m long with one tee branch, as shown on the instructor's drawing. Cut the threaded rod and strut to length, level the hangers, fit the tray and tee, then lay and tie three lengths of cable along the tray and out through a drop-out, keeping a power cable apart from a data cable. The cables are not connected to any supply. Every member builds or fits at least one hanger, and each lays and ties one cable. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the run is finished and the area is clean.
materials: Perforated tray, 2 lengths, with one tee and splice plates
Threaded rod, strut channel, nuts, washers and beam clamps or ceiling anchors
Three lengths of cable (two power, one data), not connected
Cable ties and a drop-out fitting or edge guard
Hacksaw, file, zinc-rich paint, spanners, spirit level, tape measure
Mobile tower or step platform as the Centre provides
photos: The trapeze hangers fixed and levelled, before the tray goes on
The tray and tee fitted on the hangers, with splice joints
Cables laid in the tray, power and data kept apart
The drop-out fitting where the cables leave the tray
The work area cleaned, with off-cuts in the scrap bin
checklist: Wore the right PPE and used the access equipment safely
Cut rod and strut to length and removed burrs
Fixed hangers secure and level, at the spacing given
Fitted the tray and tee with splice plates and all bolts tight
Laid cables neatly with no twists, keeping power and data apart
Tied cables at regular spacing and kept to the bending radius
Protected the cables where they leave the tray and labelled each end
Left the area clean and returned tools and spare materials
safety: Lock the tower wheels before climbing; never over-reach
Wear safety glasses when cutting rod or strut, and gloves when handling cut metal
Keep tools and fixings in a bag or tray while working overhead
Put up a barrier below the work area
The bay and cables are not connected to any supply during this task
